title: Bridging-based ranking
lede: Bridging-based ranking scores content by how much it is liked across groups that usually disagree, instead of by raw popularity. It is the idea behind X's Community Notes algorithm and the consensus scoring in Polis.

sections.heading: Play it
sections.body:
44 raters, three notes. Drag how much each camp likes each note, then make one camp bigger.

Majority vote

Share of all raters: helpful

Bridging

A approval × B approval

Bridging score is Polis's group-informed consensus: each camp's approval is (helpful + 1) / (ratings + 2), and the two are multiplied, so one camp saying no sinks a note. The four middle raters join the nearer camp. The brigade is 15 accounts that join Camp B and rate only Camp B's favorite helpful.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body:
Bridging-based ranking scores an item by how much it is liked across groups that usually disagree, instead of by how many people like it. Aviv Ovadya and Luke Thorburn call the wider family bridging systems: systems "which increase mutual understanding and trust across divides" [1].

Popularity ranking (likes, upvotes, a majority vote) rewards whatever the largest or most active group wants, which is the old [[Tyranny of the majority]] problem in a feed. A bridging ranker asks a different question: would people who normally disagree both accept this? A note that only one side loves scores low no matter how big that side is.

The best known deployment ranks fact-checking notes on X. The team that built it described an algorithm that finds annotations "that appeal broadly across heterogeneous user groups" [2]. By 2026 the same idea sat under crowd fact-checking at several large platforms, which a 2026 ICML paper lists as "X, Meta, TikTok and Google" [3].

sections.heading: How Community Notes scores a note
sections.body:
[[Community Notes]] (called Birdwatch until 2022) lets contributors write notes on posts and rate other people's notes. Notes are shown "by a bridging-based algorithm not based on majority rule" [1].

The ranker is a small [[Matrix factorization]] model. Each rating is predicted as the sum of four parts:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| μ | a global baseline |
| i_u | how generous this rater is |
| i_n | the note intercept: how helpful the note is to everyone |
| f_u × f_n | agreement explained by viewpoint: rater and note each get one number on a learned axis |

The model is fit to minimize squared error plus a penalty on the parameters, and the intercepts are penalized five times harder (0.15) than the factors (0.03). So the fit explains as much as it can with the viewpoint axis first, and "for a note to achieve a high intercept term (which is the note's helpfulness score), it must be rated helpful by raters with a diversity of viewpoints" [2].

A note needs an intercept of 0.40 or more to be marked Helpful and shown on the post [3], and its factor must be small (under 0.50 in size), so a note loved by one side cannot pass on intensity alone. The code and the rating data are public: "The algorithm used to rank Community Notes and compute their statuses is open-source" [4].

sections.heading: Two camps, one note
Fit the model yourself
sections.body:
Tap a rating to flip it (helpful, not helpful, no rating). The model is never told who is in which camp; it has to find the axis from the ratings.

note interceptnote factor
helpful✗not helpfulno rating

Fit: 1,500 steps of plain gradient descent (step 0.01) on r̂ = μ + iu + in + fu·fn, minimizing squared error plus 0.15 × (μ² + iu² + in²) plus 0.03 × (fu² + fn²), the loss and weights Community Notes documents. Helpful = 1, not helpful = 0. Same seeded start every time, so it is deterministic; the factor's sign is arbitrary, so we flip it to put Camp A on the left. "Helpful" applies the real rule (in ≥ 0.40 and |fn| < 0.50) to a toy of 8 raters, where μ also absorbs whatever every note shares.

sections.heading: What the studies found
sections.body:
| Study | Data | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Wojcik et al. 2022, X's own team | survey experiment plus the live rollout | people shown bridging-selected notes "were significantly less likely to reshare" the post [1] |
| Andreou and Sirivianos 2026 | 212.9 million ratings, 2.33 million notes | one viewpoint axis is too few; a second axis, read as trust in institutions, predicts unseen ratings [2] |
| Selvam et al. 2026, with X staff | historical production data | up to 10.7% of lower quality notes could be pushed over the threshold with fewer than 10 ratings [3] |

The first result is the case for bridging: a note chosen this way changes behavior, not only opinions. The second says the production model is too simple, since people who agree on left and right can still split on institutions. The third, written with X engineers, led to fixes that were "developed and deployed" in the live algorithm [3].

sections.heading: Weak spots
sections.body:
- **Speed.** Waiting for both sides to rate takes time. A CSCW 2024 study found no evidence that the rollout cut engagement with misleading posts and concluded notes "might be too slow" for the most viral early hours [1].
- **Coverage.** Most notes are never shown. A 2025 analysis puts the share rated helpful at "low, 10%, and declining" [2].
- **Manipulation at small scale.** A simulation found that "a small minority (5--20%) of bad raters" can suppress targeted helpful notes [3]. Coordinated fake accounts are a [[Sybil attack]] on the viewpoint axis.
- **Needing enough raters.** The model must place each rater and note on the axis from ratings alone. Community Notes' own documentation says that where few ratings exist "matrix factorization is forced to estimate the note intercept based on the limited data available" [4], which makes scores swing as new ratings arrive.

sections.heading: Polis: bridging for a room
sections.body:
[[Polis]] is the small-scale relative, built for public consultations such as Taiwan's vTaiwan. Participants vote agree, disagree or pass on short statements; the software groups similar voters and surfaces statements "about which all the diverse clusters agree" [1].

Its ranking needs no model fitting. For each opinion group, estimate the chance a member agrees as (agrees + 1) / (votes + 2), then multiply across groups; the product "will be highest for comments every group tends to agree with" [2]. This is the score on the Bridging scoreboard above. Because it is a product, "even a single small group united in opposition" can hold a statement down [3].

The catch is the grouping. The Polis authors note that the metric "can vary significantly based on what the chosen opinion groups look like" [4], so whoever picks the clustering method shapes the result.

sections.heading: What it cannot do
sections.body:
Agreement across groups is not the same as truth. Community Notes states its own target plainly: notes "that are found helpful to people from a wide variety of perspectives" [1]. A claim both camps wrongly believe passes; a correct note that one camp rejects does not. Simulations find the algorithm "suppresses a substantial fraction of genuinely helpful notes" [2].

It also depends on who counts as a side. With a single left and right axis, disagreement on anything else goes unseen: in the 2026 refit, notes that split raters on the second axis were published far less often, and in a one-axis fit "the information that raters at one end of the second axis support them is lost" [3].

Used well, bridging is a filter against one group outvoting another, which is a different question from the one [[Wisdom of the crowd]] answers. It still needs sources, experts and time to decide what is actually true. See also [[Filter bubble]].
